1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5.name: Benko Gambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5.background: B. Argunov analysed 3...b5 in the second 1946 issue of Shakhmaty v SSSR, written in a city on the Volga, which gave the opening its Eastern European name, the Volga Gambit. Pal Benko promoted it from the late 1960s, and his name stuck in English-speaking countries.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5.strategy: Offers a pawn to undermine the base of White's pawn chain. Black wants half-open a- and b-files, an unblocked long diagonal for the g7-bishop and a single kingside pawn island: long-term pressure rather than a quick attack, with White having to defend an extra pawn patiently.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6.name: Benoni Defence: Modern Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6.background: Max Euwe named it the "Tal-System" in his 1965 opening encyclopedia, in recognition of Mikhail Tal's contribution to it. Down 2-0 in the 1972 world championship match, Bobby Fischer answered Spassky's 1.d4 with it in Game 3 and won.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6.strategy: Strikes at the tip of the pawn chain and invites ...exd5. White then has a central pawn majority and a target on d6, Black a queenside majority, an open e-file and the dark squares. A sharp, imbalanced game in which Black plays for the win.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 d6.name: Benoni Defence: Hromádka System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 d6.strategy: Develops first and delays the fight against the pawn chain. The pawn keeps White's e-pawn from advancing to e5 with gain of time, frees d7 for the queen's knight and leaves time for ...g6, ...Bg7 and castling; Black decides later how to break the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5.name: Benoni Defence: Czech Benoni Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5.background: Also known as the Hromádka Benoni, after Karel Hromádka.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5.strategy: Closes the centre and gives up the fight against the pawn chain. Black is left cramped and passive: White has lasting space and chooses which wing to open, while Black manoeuvres and prepares a break with ...b5 or ...f5 that White can often prevent.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 Ne4.name: Vulture Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 Ne4.background: Stefan Bücker gave it its name when he published analysis of it and two other Benoni lines in 1989. By 1998 it had become quite popular.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 Ne4.strategy: Centralises the knight at once, aiming to hold e4 or bring it round to d6 for ...f5. But the knight can be driven away with tempo, Black falls behind in development, and White usually keeps a comfortable edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5.strategy: Accepts the pawn, the principal answer: declining brings problems of its own, since it allows Black to expand with ...b4 or keep the tension. White takes material and must then show that the extra pawn survives Black's lasting pressure on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.Nf3.name: Benko Gambit Declined: Main Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.Nf3.strategy: The main way of declining: White develops and keeps the choice of when to capture on b5. Black can expand with ...b4, but more often fianchettoes and lets play return to something close to the accepted gambit, with White's knight already developed.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.a4.name: Benko Gambit Declined: Sosonko Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.a4.strategy: Goes after the b5 pawn at once: with a4 and c4 both attacking it, Black cannot leave it there and must resolve the tension, by taking on c4, advancing it or checking on a5. A serious try that leads to sharp play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.Bg5.name: Benko Gambit Declined: Bishop Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.Bg5.strategy: Aims at the f6 knight and develops outside the pawn chain, but ignores the gambit: the c4 pawn can simply be taken with ...bxc4, and the bishop has no strong follow-up. Playable, yet Black gets a free hand on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.f3.name: Benko Gambit Declined: Pseudo-Sämisch
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 with a pawn and takes e4 and g4 away from Black's knight, but leaves the c4 pawn to be taken with ...bxc4 and loosens the king's diagonal. It builds a centre at the cost of time, and gains less than other ways of declining.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.Nd2.name: Benko Gambit Declined: Quiet Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.Nd2.strategy: The quiet way to decline: the knight guards c4 and supports e4, so if Black takes on c4 White builds a centre and recovers the pawn with the bishop. Solid, but the knight blocks the c1-bishop and Black can still gain queenside space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.e4.name: Benko Gambit Declined: Hjørring Countergambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.e4.strategy: A countergambit that offers the e-pawn to meet Black's flank play with a central blow. Taking with ...b4 or ...bxc4 lets e5 hit the knight with tempo; ...Nxe4 is the safe capture, and then White has only a level game. Sound, but it gains nothing if Black answers correctly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.g4.name: Benko Gambit: Mutkin Countergambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.g4.strategy: Offers a pawn for a kingside attack, but nothing guards g4 and ...Nxg4 simply takes it. White is undeveloped and has given a pawn away with little to show for it before the fight has started.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6.name: Benko Gambit Accepted
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6.background: In his 1974 book, Benko used the name Benko Gambit for 3...b5 4.cxb5 a6 and Volga Gambit for 3...b5 on its own; today the two names are used interchangeably.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6.strategy: The gambit proper, essentially the only move: Black offers a second pawn to open the a-file as well as the b-file. If White takes, Black cannot win both pawns back at once but gets half-open files against the queenside, an open long diagonal and a compact pawn structure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 Qa5+.strategy: Checks in order to win back the pawn at once, but 5.Nc3 blocks the check and defends b5. Black has spent a move, is still a pawn down and has not opened the a-file, which is what the gambit is for.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 Bb7.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d5, which only the queen guards, so White has to defend it at once. But the gambit needs ...a6 and the open a-file, and with the bishop already committed White can hold the extra pawn with Nc3 and e4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.bxa.name: Benko Gambit Accepted: Fully Accepted Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.bxa.strategy: Takes the second pawn: White is two pawns up for the moment and Black can win only one back at once. The question to Black is direct: are the open a- and b-files, the long diagonal and the lead in development worth the material?

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.f3.name: Benko Gambit Accepted: Dlugy Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.f3.background: Has been gaining in popularity in recent years, as the newer way for White to half-accept the gambit.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.f3.strategy: Declines the second pawn and prepares e4 with the f-pawn instead of a knight, so White can build a centre quickly. The price is a loosened king's diagonal, which Black can use for a time-gaining check on a5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.e3.name: Benko Gambit Accepted: Modern Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.e3.background: The older way to half-accept the gambit, covered in Benko's own book and in major opening treatises since; it remains popular at all levels.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop so that it can recapture on b5, keeping the extra pawn in a compact set-up. Black can play against the loose d5 pawn, or keep the tension and develop with a fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.b6.name: Benko Gambit Accepted: Pawn Return Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.b6.background: Popular at the grandmaster level as of 2004, and considered safer for Black.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.b6.strategy: Returns the pawn at once: Black regains it on b6 and the material is level. White avoids defending an extra pawn through the middlegame but also gives up the point of the gambit, a quiet choice that leaves Black comfortable.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.Nc3.name: Benko Gambit: Zaitsev System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and does not grab the second pawn. After ...axb5 the knight supports a quick e4 that takes space and shores up d5, so White fights for the centre instead of the extra material. The positions are sharp and double-edged.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.bxa.strategy: Regains a pawn and puts the bishop on the diagonal to f1: if White later plays e3 or e4, Black can take the f1-bishop and force the king to recapture, ruining castling. White also has the open a- and b-files to worry about.

Fianchettoes first and keeps the choice of how to take on a6, since the knight may do it as well as the bishop. It is aimed at White's double fianchetto: after b3 and Bb2, ...Nxa6 and ...Nb4 hit d5 and a2. Slightly less direct than recapturing at once.

A sideline that hits d5 before White can reinforce it with e4. Once the pawn is traded off, c6 is free for the knight and the centre opens. Black still has to win back a6, so the play is for activity, not structure.

The natural developing move: the knight supports e4 and brings White's pieces towards the centre. White is still behind in development and has to solve the problem of the f1-bishop, which the bishop on a6 makes awkward.

Fianchettoes the king's bishop, so the f1-bishop's problem is solved by moving it before ...Bxf1 can be forced, and White castles normally. The bishop is passive, blocked by White's own pawn on d5, but the set-up is solid and Black has to win the queenside by manoeuvring.

Prepares the double fianchetto: the queen's bishop on b2 takes the long diagonal and the king's bishop follows on g2. It avoids the f1-bishop problem, but White spends time on a slow set-up while Black's pieces come out freely against the queenside.
A solid developing move: it controls e5, frees d7 for the queen's knight and prepares ...g6 and ...Bg7. If White plays e4, Black can take the f1-bishop and force White to castle artificially.

The same set-up in another order: the king's bishop heads for the long diagonal and the d-pawn can wait. If White plays e4, the f1-bishop is still taken, so the pressure that makes up for the pawn stays.

Puts the queen on a5 to pressure c3 and a2 at once and tie White's pieces to their defence. The queen can become a target, and ...d6 and the fianchetto, the real development of the position, still wait.

Develops the knight and avoids the double fianchetto. Black recaptures on a6 with the bishop, and the game reaches the usual structures with White still having to solve the f1-bishop and Black having pressure on the queenside files.

Heads for the double fianchetto, the set-up 5...g6 is made to meet: after ...Bg7 and Bb2, Black takes on a6 with the knight and goes to b4, hitting d5 and a2. Nc3 then runs into ...Nfxd5, so White struggles to keep both the extra pawn and the centre.

Fianchettoes the king's bishop to sidestep the problem of the f1-bishop, but the bishop is blocked by White's own pawn on d5. Black recaptures on a6 with the piece that suits the set-up and keeps the pressure on the queenside files.

Takes back the pawn with the bishop, which now eyes the f1-bishop's diagonal and makes e3 or e4 awkward for White. Black has the fianchetto already in place and aims at the queenside files for compensation.

Finishes the fianchetto and delays the recapture: if White pushes the pawn to a7, the rook takes it. Black puts development first, so the compensation comes from piece play and the open files, while White gets time to finish development.

Recaptures with the knight, which stays on the rim and does not trouble the f1-bishop, so White builds a full centre at leisure. Black is still a pawn down and has less pressure on the queenside to show for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 b5 4.cxb5 a6 5.Nc3.strategy: Recaptures and opens the a-file against the a2 pawn. White's knight can take on b5, but the usual plan is to ignore it and build a centre, which leaves Black pressure on the file and a pawn to challenge the knight.

Develops the bishop but loses a tempo if White takes on a6: the bishop needs a second move to recapture. White can also decline with e4 and, after ...axb5, keep the extra pawn with Bxb5. Black has little to show for the lost time.

Delays the recapture and fianchettoes, hoping White takes on a6. White declines with e4: after ...axb5, Bxb5 keeps the extra pawn, so Black depends on White's cooperation and has spent a move for nothing.
Takes the centre instead of the b5 pawn: e4 supports d5 and gives White space, to smother Black's queenside play with a mobile pawn centre. The cost is a knight on c3 that the b-pawn can now harass.

Takes the pawn with the knight and keeps the extra pawn for now. But the knight is attacked at once by ...Ba6 and must be defended or moved, which costs time, while Black's pieces come out and the a-file stays open against a2.

Develops without committing the centre pawns, but lets Black drive the knight back with ...b4 at once. White gets a calm game rather than the central grip that e4 gives, and Black's queenside play proceeds unhindered.

Attacks the knight and drives it away from its support of e4 and d5. The game turns sharp: the knight has few good squares and White's centre becomes a target, but Black has to prove the move is worth the time.
Grabs the e4 pawn but loses the knight: Nxe4 takes it, and Black has only a pawn for a piece.

Ignores the attack on b5: White takes the pawn with the knight and Black is a pawn down, with only some activity to show for it. The tempo-gaining ...b4 that drives the knight back is the point of the position.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and prepares e4, taking central space against Black's closed centre. With the pawn on d5 secure, White can build a broad centre and later choose which wing to open.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, but it can be driven off at once: ...e4 hits it, and after it retreats Black has gained space and time in the centre. White loses the quiet build-up that Nc3 and e4 give and no longer has a clear advantage.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.g3.strategy: Prepares the king's bishop on g2, a quiet development that guards the king and the d5 pawn from behind. It does not fight for the centre or prepare e4 quickly, so Black gets time for ...d6 and the queenside break.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6.strategy: Shores up the e5 pawn with a solid chain and keeps the centre closed. Black has little space and has to wait for the right moment to break with ...b5 or ...f5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop and keeps ...d6 for when the pawn is needed. Black accepts the closed centre and cramped space and relies on a later ...f5 or ...b5, since the e5 pawn blocks the bishop's diagonal in the meantime.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on queenside play before the centre is settled: it prepares ...b5 and takes that square from White's knight. White can use the time to take space with e4, and the move does nothing for the cramped kingside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6 5.e4.strategy: Takes much more space and gives the pawn on d5 a firm base. White can now play for kingside expansion or a break on either flank, while Black's position stays passive and cramped.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and puts e5 under pressure, keeping e4 and a kingside fianchetto both in hand. White gains less space at once, but Black's pieces have few good squares and Black must wait for the right moment to break.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6 5.g3.strategy: A fianchetto set-up: the bishop on g2 guards d5 from behind, and e4 can follow later. White gives up the immediate grab for space, so Black can castle and prepare the break at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6 5.e4 g.name: Benoni Defence: King's Indian System
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6 5.e4 g.strategy: Fianchettoes the king's bishop instead of developing it on e7. The bishop is hemmed in by its own pawn on e5, so the plan is slower than the usual development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6 5.e4 B.strategy: The natural, solid development: the bishop stands safely behind the e5-d6 chain and Black castles next. Black accepts a cramped position and plans ...b5 or ...f5 only once the pieces are in place, while White holds the space and chooses where to play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e5 4.Nc3 d6 5.e4 N.strategy: Reinforces e5 and prepares ...f5 or a knight route to c5, but it boxes in the queen's bishop and leaves the king's bishop no better square than e7. Playable, if passive.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and prepares e4 to support the d5 pawn. If Black waited, White could recapture on d5 with the e-pawn and keep space without giving Black a queenside majority, so Black usually takes at once.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight first and keeps c3 free. It lets Black try a pawn sacrifice with ...b5, and the knight blocks the f-pawn, so the sharp f-pawn attacks of the main line are off. If Black takes on d5, the main structure usually arises.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.g3.strategy: Prepares a kingside fianchetto instead of a central build-up. After ...exd5 and cxd5 the set-up is solid and positional, but it puts no immediate question to Black, who can develop and start the queenside play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5.strategy: Takes at once so that White cannot recapture with the e-pawn later. This creates the opening's imbalance: White gets a big centre and the first initiative, Black a queenside majority and counterplay, in a sharper game than delaying the capture would give.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 d6.strategy: Keeps the tension and heads for the fianchetto instead of taking on d5. If White builds with e4, Black can take later and let White recapture with the e-pawn: that costs the queenside majority but avoids the big pawn centre of the main line, and the game stays solid and balanced.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 g6.strategy: Heads for the fianchetto first and keeps the capture on d5 in hand. If White plays e4, Black can still take and let White recapture with the e-pawn, which keeps White's space but removes the pawn centre of the main line. A sound, flexible alternative to ...d6.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cx.strategy: Recaptures with the c-pawn, as the structure demands: White has a central majority and a space advantage, Black a queenside majority and a half-open e-file. The pawn on d5 cramps Black, who must find activity.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.Nx.strategy: Regains the pawn by trading knights and recapturing with the queen, so material is level. But there is no cramping pawn on d5 any more, and the queen comes out early and may lose time as Black develops.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.Qx.strategy: Loses the queen: Black takes it with the knight, and White gets only a knight and a pawn for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cx.strategy: The standard move: it stops White's d-pawn from advancing to d6 and prepares the bishop's fianchetto on g7, which brings Black control of the central dark squares. The price is a backward pawn on d6 for White to aim at.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cx.name: Benoni Defence: Modern Variation, Snake Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cx.background: Rolf Olav Martens invented it in 1982 and named it for the sinuous movement of the bishop; the Swedish word for snake, orm, is an anagram of his initials. Normunds Miezis has been a regular exponent.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cx.strategy: An unusual development: the bishop goes to d6 instead of g7, keeping the d-pawn at home and sidestepping the weakness on d6. But it gives up the long diagonal that makes the usual set-up work, and White keeps an edge.

Fianchettoes at once but leaves d6 to White: 6.d6 puts a pawn on the sixth rank that cramps Black's development and costs time to win back. The usual ...d6 stops that advance; this order only gives White an extra option.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cx.name: Benoni Defence: King's Pawn Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cx.strategy: Builds the full centre and gains space, putting Black's set-up to the test. The price is a half-open e-file, which gives Black a target and counterplay against the pawn.

Develops the knight and takes e5 from Black's pieces, without committing the e-pawn. Sound, and White keeps the space, but Black reaches the fianchetto and castling without facing a full pawn centre, so White has less than with e4.
Fianchettoes the king's bishop: it guards d5 and e4 and the king, so Black has no obvious target. The set-up is slow, so White plays for a small, lasting space advantage rather than an attack.

Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop, which will bear down the long diagonal on White's centre and the dark squares. Black accepts a weak pawn on d6 and relies on active play and queenside pressure.

Takes b5 from White's bishop and prepares ...b5, but spends a tempo while the pieces are still at home. White answers with f4, a broad centre with the threat of e5, or shuts the queenside with a4, and Black is behind in the fight for the centre.

Develops the queen's knight towards e5 and keeps Black's plans open. It takes the f6-knight's retreat square on d7, though, and walks into a pin by Bb5, so Black has to watch for a quick e4-e5 or a kingside pawn advance by White.
